---
title: "Snaps, Flatpak and Other Software Formats"
---

A host can have multiple software inventories. A program named `firefox` or `editor` may be provided by a Debian package, a Snap, a Flatpak, or a file installed by an administrator. Updating only APT does not update every one of them.

## Identify the owner and update path

APT and dpkg manage Debian packages and their dependencies. Snap packages are managed by snapd, with revisions, channels, interfaces and a separate refresh mechanism. Flatpak applications and shared runtimes are managed per system or per user through configured remotes. Standalone binaries, language-specific environments and container images have still other owners and update paths. A container image is not a replacement for updating the host kernel or runtime.

Start by identifying a particular command instead of guessing its format:

```bash
type -a firefox
command -v firefox
readlink -f "$(command -v firefox)"
```

If the command is missing, `command -v` returns nonzero and there is no resolved path to inspect. A launcher or wrapper may hand off to another manager; a Debian-owned launcher does not prove the application payload is a Debian package. Follow the actual execution path and compare inventories:

```bash
dpkg-query -S /usr/bin/firefox
snap list
flatpak list
```

The example path may be absent or unowned; the `snap` or `flatpak` commands may not be installed. Run the relevant query only when its manager exists, and inspect the path actually found. Manager inventory and application behavior both matter.

## Snap: revisions, confinement and refresh

Where snapd is installed, inspect without installing or changing anything:

```bash
snap list --all
snap refresh --time
snap changes
```

A Snap has a publisher, channel and revision; `snap list --all` may show retained disabled revisions. Snaps normally refresh automatically. Strict confinement uses interfaces to mediate access, whereas classic confinement grants broader host access; confinement is not a guarantee that an application is safe. A refresh can affect running services or application sessions. [Snap's update documentation](https://snapcraft.io/docs/how-to-guides/manage-snaps/manage-updates/) explains schedules, holds and their scope.

A targeted refresh can bypass a hold on that specific snap; do not treat a hold as an immutable freeze. Reverting to a retained revision can restore some revision-specific data, but common application data and external databases can remain changed. Test the application's own recovery procedure and compatibility before relying on a revert. See [Snap revisions](https://snapcraft.io/docs/revisions/) for data behavior.

## Flatpak: applications, runtimes and remotes

If Flatpak is installed, inventory both applications and runtimes, and distinguish the user and system installations:

```bash
flatpak remotes --show-details
flatpak list --app
flatpak list --runtime
```

A remote is a software source with its own trust and lifecycle. An application can depend on a runtime maintained separately from the host's Debian libraries. Permissions and desktop portals mediate access, but available grants and overrides change the effective boundary. Inspect an installed application's declared permissions with `flatpak info --show-permissions APP_ID`; use an actual application ID from the inventory. See [Flatpak's concepts](https://docs.flatpak.org/en/latest/basic-concepts.html) and [command reference](https://docs.flatpak.org/en/latest/flatpak-command-reference.html).

No installation or permission change is required for this exercise. On a server, avoid installing an additional manager simply to run these queries. Missing tools and empty lists are legitimate inventory results.

## Make one maintenance inventory

For each application record its executable or launch method, manager, publisher/source, version or revision, automatic update policy, data location, privileges, restart needs and removal/restore method. Do not assume `apt remove` removes a Snap or that removing an application removes its data. A script in `/usr/local`, a language virtual environment or a vendor tarball may have no central update service at all; assign an owner and patch process explicitly.

## Worked diagnosis and practice

A desktop application is reported vulnerable after `apt upgrade` succeeds. Determine which application is actually launched, inspect its manager and source, and compare its installed revision against the publisher's advisory. Check whether a pending refresh requires the application to exit. Update using that manager's documented process in a maintenance window, then verify the running application. On the lab clone, create a two-column inventory of installed managers and sources; explain what each manager does **not** update.
